fields.title: How much money can actually be made here
fields.keyTakeaway: Calculate bottom-up: the number of clients you can actually serve multiplied by the average check. A top-down estimate carved out as a percentage from a large market report crumbles under the first question.
fields.checkQuestion: "The warehouse software market is 20 billion, let us take 1%". What is wrong with this calculation?
fields.blocks/0/text: Key node question: **what growth limitations exist if nothing changes?** This question is not for investors, but for you: it shows when your current strategy hits a ceiling.
fields.blocks/1/text: **What happens if you do not answer the question.** The team grows sales, hits a wall, and does not understand why. The wall was visible in advance: the serviceable segment turned out to be several times smaller than assumed.
fields.blocks/2/subtitle: Three distinct questions, not three numbers in a row
fields.blocks/2/items/0: **TAM** — total spending on this problem in principle. Needed to understand if there is a business here at all.
fields.blocks/2/items/1: **SAM** — spending by those you can actually reach: your geography, customer size, sales channel.
fields.blocks/2/items/2: **SOM** — what you will realistically capture over a foreseeable period given your team and channel.
fields.blocks/2/items/3: **Calculate bottom-up:** number of customers × average check × frequency. Top-down is only for sanity-checking the order of magnitude.
fields.blocks/3/text:
Top-down: nationwide warehouse software market is 20 billion rubles a year; "taking 1%" gives 200 million. A nice, useless number: it includes factories, retail chains, and customs warehouses that Kedr cannot sell to.

Bottom-up: there are about 9,000 distributors in the country with 5 to 50 warehouse workers. About half already have automated warehouses, making them unreachable in the coming years. That leaves 4,500. At a check of 40 thousand a month, SAM is about 2.2 billion a year.

SOM: a sales team of four closes 6 deals a month with a two-month cycle. Over two years, that is 144 clients — about 69 million a year.

The second calculation is uncomfortable yet useful: it proves the ceiling is dictated by sales team capacity, not market size.
fields.blocks/4/text: Most often, the constraint is the sales channel, not the number of potential clients. A bottom-up calculation reveals this immediately, while a top-down model hides it.
fields.blocks/4/title: The ceiling is rarely the market
fields.blocks/5/text: Market sizing is an exercise in assumptions: shift a segment boundary, and the figure triples. That is why documented assumptions matter more than final numbers. Plus, market size says nothing about whether clients will choose to pay you specifically.
